comments.text: @30:00 como psicologa deberias saber de que los pacientes muchas veces mienten. Los pacientes suicidas a veces te dicen que estan bien, los pacientes adictos a veces te manipulan para justificarse, los que tienen desordenes de dismorfia como bulimia y anorexia constantemente tratan de hacerte validar sus visiones torcidas de si mismas. La salud mental es complicada, porque en si cuando terapistas profesionales con mas años de experiencia vieron el caso, recogieron el testimonio de la terapista de lo que se hablo en su consulta, y revisaron lo que le prescribio, dijeron que ella fue pragmatica y correcta en lo que hizo. Aparte de eso uno tiene que escuchar a sus pacientes y corres el riesgo a que este este ocultando algo. En ese sentido mucho se ha hablado del sistema de salud de los Estados Unidos, pero este no es un caso de la salud o de las compañias farmacéuticas. A veces si hay neglicencia pero la unica y mayor falla en este caso fue que los profesionales que la vieron, no se comunicaron entre ellos. Pero incluso pensando en ello, a estos profesionales no se les hacia tan facil saber que ella estaba viendo a otros profesionales. Recuerden que las consultas a las que ella iba eran practica privada. Ellos tenian dinero, el esposo hacia 40 mil dolares por mes. Cuando tenia 20 años mi sueldo anual no llegaba a los 40 mil dolares. Patrick hacia medio millon de dolares al año. Es mas dificil para los profesionales de la salud revisar o saber los diagnosticos, otros profesionales trabajando con ella, los medicamentos que esta tomaba, etc cuando tienen practicas privadas que cuando trabajan con un programa público como medicare o medicaid. No digo que sea imposible, pero no siempre uno asume que la o el paciente esta siendo visto por otros.

comments.text: I live part of the year in Chile, and the rest in Switzerland, and I can still do not understand how average chileans manage to cover all the costs they have... that is one reason why almost everyone is always in debt (credit cards), and even for us, coming from one of the most expensive countries in the world, it is puzzling that so many things cost almost as much as in Switzerland. BUT if you know WHERE to buy, you can still get much better prices, also when you buy in "big" quantities (from 6 units up). We use both strategies. There are still some things that are frankly cheap and good, for instance wine, and transportation. Too bad that in later years uncontrolled immigration has also increased the crime rate (which used to be low), but again if you know where to go and where not to go and also are alert and have a good sense of judging contexts and situations, you can still travel quite without incidents. In any case the scenery and variety of landscapes is SUPERB, and still with a wild and pristine nature in most of the country. In any case Chile is very rich in resources, especially very valued ones (strategic minerals, all alternative energy resources, marine resources, CLEAN WATER (the big ice fields and Antarcrtica), a bright future in geospatial sciences and astronomy) but above all it also has a very strategic geopolitical position (a tricontinental country), this considering Southamerica and the World at large. With better politicians, entrepreneurs and a better educated average citizen, Chile could have a very high standard of living (already one of the best in the region) and certainly also be one of the best places to make a life! (otherwise I would choose its "sister country": NZ)

comments.author: @albertovillanueva5881
comments.text:
Real estate is expensive because Chile lacks space for housing in the most wanted areas. Flat land is scarce, and the south consists almost entirely of hills upon hills. From west to east, the landscape runs from the very narrow coastal strip to the Coastal Range, after that you reach the Central Valley, and finally the Andes Mountains. There is hardly any room left for construction. Furthermore, building costs are higher due to our anti-seismic regulations, which make a house cost 20% more than in other countries...On top of that, many cities are built at river mouths (making wetlands very common) and construction is imposible in these areas, which cause less available land.
By the way, good documentary...

comments.author: @ExploreTravelDocs
comments.text: I’ve traveled through Chile, and what surprised me most was how different everyday life feels from one end of the country to the other. I remember sitting near the coast with that cold Pacific air, then later seeing the Andes rising behind Santiago—it almost felt like two completely different worlds. But the thing that stayed with me was the warmth of the people. The food, the family gatherings, the long conversations over once… those little moments made Chile feel less like a place I was visiting and more like a place I could actually call home. This video brought back a lot of those memories.
